paper_title: Kandinsky 6.0 Video: Foundation Models for Synchronized Video and Audio Generation

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: We present Kandinsky 6.0 Video, a family of foundation diffusion models for synchronized text-to-audio-video generation, comprising Kandinsky 6.0 Video Lite (3B parameters) and Kandinsky 6.0 Video Pro (29B parameters). Both models generate 5-second video clips with synchronized 44 kHz audio, including lip-sync, in text-to-audio-video (T2AV) and image-to-audio-video (I2AV) modes; a built-in super-resolution model raises the output resolution to Full-HD (1920$\times$1080). Building on the video generation capabilities of Kandinsky 5.0, Kandinsky 6.0 Video employs a dual-stream CrossDiT architecture that connects a pretrained video stream and a newly trained audio stream through bidirectional cross-attention for temporal and semantic alignment. Our continuous pretraining strategy first trains the audio stream from scratch on large-scale audio corpora and then trains both streams jointly on paired audio-video data while preserving unimodal fidelity; pretraining is followed by supervised fine-tuning, reinforcement-learning-based post-training, and distillation. In side-by-side human evaluation, Kandinsky 6.0 Video Pro clearly outperforms its predecessor, Kandinsky 5.0 Video Pro, and remains competitive with leading audio-video generation models, particularly in speech quality. To accelerate open research and deployment in multimedia generation, we release the code, model checkpoints, and diffusers integration under the MIT license.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Diffusion models [1, 2] and flow matching methods [3] have proven effective for image synthesis [4, 5], offering fine detail and controllability. Extending them to video generation has required specialized architectures based on diffusion transformers (DiT) [6] and efficient spatiotemporal attention mechanisms that model temporal dependencies without prohibitive computational cost. Today, text-to-video (T2V) generation is represented by both closed-source systems (Sora [7], Veo [8]) and open-source models (HunyuanVideo [9], Wan [10], Kandinsky 5.0 [11]). Kandinsky 5.0, in particular, combines the CrossDiT architecture with sparse NABLA attention [12] to achieve high efficiency with modest computational resources. Generating video with synchronized audio (text-to-audio-video, T2AV) is substantially more challenging than generating either modality alone, as it requires semantic, temporal, and emotional consistency across modalities. Closed commercial systems such as Veo 3.1 [8], Sora 2 [13], and Wan 2.6 [10] achieve impressive results in unified audio-visual synthesis, including natural lip synchronization, dynamic background sounds, and multilingual speech. However, their source code is unavailable, hindering reproducibility and further research. Recent works target joint audio-video generation within single architecture, including ALIVE [14], SyncFlow [15], JavisDiT [16], 3MDiT [17], LTX-2 and its successor LTX-2.5 [18], MiniMaxH3 [19], and NVIDIA Cosmos 3 [20]. These models align the modalities temporally and semantically through mechanisms ranging from bidirectional cross-attention and hierarchical synchronization to flow-based architectures and omnimodal transformers. Considerable effort has also gone into scaling model size (to about 30B parameters and beyond), supporting additional input modes (image conditioning, multiple references), and developing standardized benchmarks for synchronization and quality, such as VABench [21], T2AV-Compass [22], and AVGen-Bench [23]. Despite this progress, open-source solutions still lag behind closed ones in clip duration, resolution, and synchronization accuracy, keeping this area highly active and open to new approaches. Continuing this research, we present Kandinsky 6.0 Video, family of foundation diffusion models for synchronized text-to-audio-video generation. Our contributions are as follows: We introduce two models of different scale: Kandinsky 6.0 Video Lite (3B parameters) and Kandinsky 6.0 Video Pro (29B parameters). Both generate 5-second video clips with synchronized 44 kHz audio, including lip-sync, and operate in text-to-audio-video (T2AV) and image-to-audio-video (I2AV) modes. Clips are generated in SD resolution and can be upscaled to Full-HD using built-in super-resolution model. We employ continuous pretraining strategy: the audio stream is first pretrained on large-scale audio corpora, then connected to the pretrained video stream through newly initialized cross-attention layers, and finally both streams are trained jointly on paired audio-video data. We describe multi-stage post-training pipeline consisting of domain-specific supervised fine-tuning combined via model soup, reinforcement learning adapted from OmniNFT [24], and two-stage distillation (π-Flow followed by adversarial refinement) to 10 function evaluations. We evaluate Kandinsky 6.0 Video on VABench [21] and in side-by-side human evaluation. It outperforms the open-source LTX 2.5 on most VABench metrics, clearly surpasses its predecessor, Kandinsky 5.0 Video Pro, and remains competitive with proprietary systems, particularly in speech quality. We release all model weights, source code, and integration with the diffusers library to the research community under the MIT license.

sections.title: 2 Data Processing Pipeline
sections.content: The development of Kandinsky 6.0 Video required substantial expansion of our data processing infrastructure and methodology. Building upon the foundations established for Kandinsky 5.0, we introduced novel audio modality and constructed comprehensive set of datasets for pretraining, fine-tuning, and downstream optimization. For pretraining, we prepared image (T2I), video (T2V), audio (T2A), joint audio-video (T2AV), and image-conditioned (I2AV) datasets to bootstrap the model across all modalities. For supervised fine-tuning, we developed dedicated SFT datasets for video and audio-visual tasks to enhance visual quality and achieve reliable audio-video synchronization. Additionally, we curated Reinforcement Learning dataset for online optimisation, Super-Resolution dataset to improve output detail, and an expanded Russian Cultural Code dataset to support culturally aware generation.

sections.title: 2.1 Data Processing Infrastructure
sections.content: The core data processing infrastructure was upgraded: table partitioning and load-balancing mechanisms were enhanced to support concurrent operation of thousands of data processors, and vector indexes were extended to support clustering of audio-visual embeddings.

sections.title: 2.2 Text-to-Image Dataset
sections.content: The Kandinsky T2I dataset for Kandinsky 6.0 Video is 50-million-image subset of the Kandinsky 5.0 collection, re-annotated with new captioner. Dataset Properties The subset used for Kandinsky 6.0 Video inherits the characteristics of the original Kandinsky 5.0 filtering pipeline. It consists of high-quality, diverse images with minimal text content: watermarked and text-heavy scenes were removed by the original filters, and perceptual deduplication [25] ensures broad visual variety. The dataset is balanced across object and scene categories (via YOLOv8 [26] and CLIP-based classifiers [27]), and technical and aesthetic quality scores (TOPIQ [28], Q-Align [29]) guarantee high standard. Complexity filtering (SAM 2 [30]) retains visually rich and non-trivial compositions. Content Annotation Captions are generated using Qwen3-235B-A22B [31]. Descriptions are produced in both Russian and English. Using Qwen3-30B-A3B, each description is rewritten into 4 levels of detail: long, medium, short, and shortest.

sections.title: 2.3 Text-to-Video Dataset
sections.content: For Kandinsky 6.0 Video, we selected subset of 20 million video scenes from the original Kandinsky 5.0 T2V collection. Additional filtering was applied to ensure quality and temporal consistency: clips with non-standard frame rates or containing scene transitions (detected via TransNetV2 [32]) were discarded. All selected scenes were re-captioned with new, detailed captions. 5 Dataset Properties The subset inherits the quality characteristics of the Kandinsky 5.0 pipeline while incorporating stricter temporal filtering. It consists of stable, single-scene clips without internal scene breaks, ensuring coherent visual narratives, and with standardized frame rates. Watermarks and textheavy scenes are excluded, and perceptual deduplication ensures diverse content. Technical and aesthetic quality is guaranteed by DOVER [33] and Q-Align scores, while YOLOv8 and CLIP-based classifiers maintain balance across object and scene categories. Camera and object dynamics (VideoMAE [34]) provide controlled motion diversity, and structural dynamics (MS-SSIM [35]) ensures sufficient motion without excessive redundancy. Content Annotation For the video dataset, we applied the same captioning pipeline as for images. Captions are generated using Qwen3-235B-A22B in both Russian and English. Using Qwen3-30B-A3B, each description is rewritten into 4 levels of detail: long, medium, short, and shortest. Postprocessing includes cleaning of introductory phrases and filtering of non-English and nonRussian characters.

sections.title: 2.4 Text-to-Audio Dataset
sections.content: For pretraining the audio branch, we constructed separate audio-only dataset Kandinsky T2A. It consists of 40 million audio tracks (520 seconds in length) extracted from the Kandinsky 5.0 video collection. Low-quality, silent, or corrupted tracks were discarded. Each track was annotated with textual description of its audio content using Qwen3-30B-A3B, covering sounds, music, speech, and environmental acoustics. This dataset was used to bootstrap the audio modality before joint audio-video training.

sections.title: 2.5 Text-to-Audio-Video Dataset
sections.content: For training joint video generation with sound, we constructed the Kandinsky T2AV dataset. It consists of 7 million audio-video segments derived from the Kandinsky 5.0 video collection, filtered to ensure high-quality audio, meaningful audiovisual correspondence, and suitability for lip-sync modeling. Dataset Properties The dataset was built by extracting audio tracks and applying multi-stage filtering pipeline: Audio quality filters: Scenes with silent, corrupted, or low-quality audio tracks were discarded. Remaining clips have sufficient dynamic range, low clipping ratio, and adequate amplitude. Lip-sync and synchronization filters: We applied two key metrics following the VABench benchmark [21]: Lip-Sync alignment score (LSA) and Desync. Clips with detected people were retained only if their LSA was at least 3 on scale from 0 to 5, and clips with audio-visual events were retained only if Desync was below 0.1 on scale from 0 to 1. Clips without visible faces were kept as they do not require lip-sync (about 25% of T2AV dataset). The combined filter ensures that retained clips either have good synchronization or contain no faces. Visual quality: The subset inherits the visual quality filters from the T2V pipeline (DOVER, Q-Align, CRAFT [36], YOLOv8, and CLIP-based classifiers), ensuring high-resolution, textfree, and diverse visual content. 6 Captioning Pipeline For joint audio-video training, we generated comprehensive captions describing both visual and audio content. The process involved: Extracting speech transcripts using Gemma-4-E4B-it [37], enclosed in <S>...<E> markers. Generating audio descriptions using Qwen3-30B-A3B, enclosed in <AUDCAP> ... <ENDAUDCAP> markers. Combining these components and feeding them into Qwen3.5-35B-A3B [38], which produced unified detailed caption covering both the visual scene and its accompanying audio.

sections.title: 2.6 Image-to-Audio-Video Dataset
sections.content: For the image-conditioned generation task (I2AV), we constructed dedicated dataset. It consists of 116,000 specifically selected samples derived from the Kandinsky 5.0 video collection. Each sample is pair: starting frame (first frame of video scene) and corresponding combined caption describing both the visual content of that frame and the expected audio-visual continuation. Captioning Pipeline Captions were generated using two-stage local pipeline. First, audio descriptions were produced using Gemma-4-E4B-it and Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B [39]. Second, these audio descriptions, together with camera motion classification labels, were fed into Qwen3.5-35B-A3B to produce unified video+audio caption. All captions were subsequently rewritten into four detail levels (long, medium, short, shortest) using dedicated rewriter. Dataset Properties The dataset underwent additional filtering applied to the starting frames to ensure semantic and technical suitability for image-conditioned generation. The selection criteria included: Zero-shot embedding quality (Qwen3-VL-Embedding-2B [40]): overall quality, sharpness, exposure, artifacts. No-reference image quality assessment (using PyIQA library [41]): multiple metrics including clipiqa+, topiq_nr, musiq-koniq, dbcnn, qalign, niqe, brisque, ilniqe, pi, and others. Classical CV detectors: blur detection via variance of Laplacian. Semantic suitability for I2V: Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct [42] verified that the frame represents beginning or pause of an action (not mid-action peak), that the main object is clearly visible and not cropped, and that the frame is not empty or transitional. The filtering (union of all criteria) ensured that only high-quality, semantically appropriate starting frames were retained, resulting in diverse and reliable dataset for both pretraining and subsequent fine-tuning stages. sections.title: 2.7 Supervised Fine-Tuning Datasets
sections.content: For supervised fine-tuning, we constructed two datasets: for video-only tasks and for audiovisual tasks. Both datasets share the same 11-domain taxonomy (see Table 1) and are used in two-stage training procedure: Stage 1 focuses on visual quality enhancement, Stage 2 on audio-video synchronization and lip-sync. The datasets were built with the following common pipeline: Technical quality filtering: Video scenes are filtered using DOVER, Q-Align, CRAFT, and motion dynamics models (same as in the main T2V pipeline). For audio, we apply Meta Audiobox Aesthetics [43] (production quality, complexity, content enjoyment, usefulness) and discard silent or corrupted tracks. Domain classification: Scenes are classified into 11 domains (people action, animals, cartoons, people speech, music, food, nature, art, architecture, interiors, tech) using combined visual (Qwen2.5-VL-32B-Instruct [44]) and audio (Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B) embeddings. Expert evaluation: Two-stage evaluation is performed by technical screeners and cinematography experts, with emphasis on visual aesthetics, cinematographic quality, audio clarity, semantic audio-visual alignment, and lip-sync accuracy for speech scenes. Captioning: Audio descriptions are produced with Gemma-4-E4B-it and Qwen3-Omni30B-A3B, while joint video+audio captions are generated by Qwen3.5-35B-A3B incorporating motion classification labels. All captions are subsequently rewritten into four detail levels: long, medium, short, shortest. The domain breakdown for the datasets is given in Table 1. Stage 1 (4,663 scenes) is primarily used for visual enhancement, while Stage 2 (7,686 scenes) expands the data with additional speech and music content to improve synchronization and lip-sync.

sections.title: 2.8 Reinforcement Learning Dataset
sections.content: The RL dataset comprises 2,984 curated clips sourced from the SFT collection. Each record contains T2AV-specific captions in English and Russian, with 100% of samples containing an audio caption (<AUDCAP>...<ENDAUDCAP>). Precomputed text embeddings are provided for 8 efficient online training. The dataset is used for online RL with per-prompt rollouts and multiobjective rewards.

sections.title: 2.9 Super-Resolution Data
sections.content: For super-resolution, we constructed combined dataset comprising 150,000 unique clips from three sources: 4K video collection: 100,000 diverse high-resolution video clips used to construct paired HQ/LQ examples for super-resolution training. high-resolution subset of the Kandinsky 5.0 T2V video collection, comprising approximately 35,000 clips, selected through artifact filtering and Q-Align-based quality filtering. 15,000 synthetic camera-motion clips constructed from high-resolution images from the Aesthetic-4K dataset [45]. Each clip is produced by moving spatial crop along sampled camera trajectory over still image, simulating camera motion. Quality filtering. We filter the two video datasets using different quality checks. For the Kandinsky 5.0 T2V collection, we check for compression artifacts and visible bands in smooth color gradients, and use Q-Align scores to select high-quality examples. For the 4K video collection, we combine Q-Align scores with separate ripple detector to remove low-quality examples and those with strong noise-like patterns. The preparation of paired HQ/LQ training examples, including crop selection, online filtering, and degradation pipelines, is described in Section 4.6.1.

sections.title: 2.10 Russian Cultural Code Dataset
sections.content: For Kandinsky 6.0 Video, we expanded and updated the Russian Cultural Code (RCC) dataset [46, 47]. The dataset comprises 1.2M images and 530K video scenes, specifically curated to represent the Russian cultural code covering distinctive features related to faith, language, historical memory, nature, architecture, and other culturally significant elements. All samples are annotated with accurate object names and comprehensive scene descriptions, ensuring high-quality data for culturally aware generation. The dataset is used during the T2V pre-training phase and is also injected through images during joint T2AV training, in both cases with English and Russian captions, to support the models ability to generate content that aligns with Russian cultural context.

sections.title: 3.2 Core Model
sections.content: The core of Kandinsky 6.0 Video is dual-stream CrossDiT architecture that processes the video and audio modalities, similar to Ovi [49] and LTX-2 [18]. It comprises asymmetric DiT backbones for video and audio, connected by blockwise bidirectional cross-attention. Figure 1 shows simplified scheme of single block with both streams and the crossattention that connects them; detailed diagram is given in Figure 2. Each stream inherits its architecture from Kandinsky 5.0 [11]. The two streams have the same number of transformer blocks but differ in hidden and feed-forward (FFN) dimensions and, consequently, in parameter count. In Kandinsky 6.0 Video Lite (3B parameters in total), the video stream has 2B parameters, the audio stream 0.6B, and the cross-attention layers between the streams 0.4B. In Kandinsky 6.0 Video Pro (29B in total), the video stream has 19B parameters, the audio stream 5B, and the cross-attention layers 5B. Positions are encoded with Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE) [50]: video tokens are indexed by frame number and audio tokens by temporal position. For video, the frame index is normalized by the frame rate relative to 24 fps: RoPE (cid:18) Nframe fps/24 (cid:19) , where Nframe is the input frame index and fps is the frames per second of the input video. sections.title: 3.3 Super-Resolution Model
sections.content: To obtain Full-HD output, videos generated by Kandinsky 6.0 Video are upscaled by separate video super-resolution (SR) model. Unlike the base generator, which uses the Hunyuan VAE, the SR model operates in the latent space of K-VAE [51], video autoencoder with 64 latent channels and 16 spatial and 4 temporal compression. For spatially aligned inputs 16 64, with = 4n+1 frames, clip of W pixels is encoded into latent of size where = (T 1)/4 + 1. Thus, 121-frame clip corresponds to 31 latent frames. 16 The SR model consists of two components trained separately: the Latent Upscaler (LU), convolutional network that deterministically upsamples low-quality (LQ) latent by factor of 2 or 4 to the working resolution of the SR-DiT (Section 3.3.2); the SR-DiT, flow-matching diffusion transformer that removes degradations and restores detail in the upsampled latent (Section 3.3.1). single SR-DiT is trained jointly for the 2 and 4 routes, while the LU uses scale-specific branches. In our inference pipeline, the SR-DiT processes spatial tiles (height width) corresponding to 512 768 px for landscape content, 768 512 px for portrait content, and 512 512 px for square content. These correspond to latent grids of 32 48, 48 32, and 32 32 cells, respectively, with 64 channels. For fixed scale and working tile size, larger input videos require more tiles (Section 5). sections.title: 4 Training Stages
sections.content: Figure 5: Training pipeline of Kandinsky 6.0 Video. The video stream (initialized from the pretrained Kandinsky 5.0 Video model) and the audio stream are first pre-trained separately, then fused and trained jointly in T2AV mode and in mixed T2AV/I2AV mode. Joint pre-training is followed by supervised fine-tuning with model soup, RL-based post-training, and distillation.

sections.title: 4.1 Overview
sections.content: Kandinsky 6.0 Video is trained in several sequential stages (Figure 5). Pre-training comprises three phases: separate training of the video stream, separate training of the audio stream from scratch, and joint training of both streams. Pre-training is followed by supervised finetuning (SFT), RL-based post-training (alignment), and distillation. Kandinsky 6.0 Video Lite and Kandinsky 6.0 Video Pro follow the same training scheme and differ mainly in the number of steps, batch size, and learning rates; other differences are stated where they apply (e.g., the RL setup in Section 4.4).

sections.title: 4.2 Continuous Pre-training
sections.content: All pre-training stages use flow matching [3] with an MSE loss. The audio and video streams are first trained separately and are then connected through cross-attention layers and trained jointly. The audio stream is trained from scratch, with weights randomly initialized from normal distribution. The video stream is initialized from the corresponding Kandinsky 5.0 Video (Lite or Pro) pre-training checkpoint (SD resolution, 45k steps). At each stage, the Lite and Pro models are trained on the same data. 4.2.1 Separate Training Kandinsky 6.0 Video Lite: Text-to-audio (T2A): 40k steps on T2A captions; batch size 128 640 seconds; sample length from 5 to 20 seconds. T2A (continued): 2k steps on T2AV captions; batch size 256 640 seconds; sample length from 5 to 20 seconds. Text-to-video (T2V), in parallel with T2A: starting from the Kandinsky 5.0 Video Lite SD pretraining checkpoint (45k steps on T2V captions), 20k steps of T2V pre-training on T2AV captions; batch size 2 512 = 1024. 17 Kandinsky 6.0 Video Pro: T2A: 30k steps on T2A captions; batch size 128 640 seconds. T2A (continued): 4k steps on T2AV captions; batch size 256 640 seconds. T2V, in parallel with T2A: starting from the Kandinsky 5.0 Video Pro SD pre-training checkpoint (45k steps on T2V captions), 14k steps of T2V pre-training on T2AV captions; batch size 1 1024 = 1024. 4.2.2 Joint T2AV Training Kandinsky 6.0 Video Lite: T2AV: 57.5k steps; batch size 256; up to 121 frames at 2325 fps (at most 5 seconds of video). T2AV + I2AV: 4k additional steps with learning rate 1e5, with 25% of samples in I2AV mode. Kandinsky 6.0 Video Pro: T2AV: 46k steps with learning rate 5e5, followed by 3k steps with learning rate 2.5e5 (49k steps in total). T2AV + I2AV: 5k additional steps with learning rate 2.5e5, with 25% of samples in I2AV mode. During joint T2AV training, we use the independent_time mode, in which the diffusion time is sampled independently for video and audio, so that the two modalities are noised to different levels t. This is required for audio-to-video and video-to-audio generation, where the model must take into account information from the other modality. In addition, training batch may contain audio only, video only, images only, or video with audio; images come from the image dataset, which is also used to inject knowledge of the Russian Cultural Code (RCC). Training is performed in bfloat16 precision. Training details and hyperparameters for all continuous pre-training stages are given in Table 3. 4.2.3 Image-to-Audio-Video (I2AV) Mode Both model versions are trained in I2AV mode with probability of 25% during the final pretraining stage. The input scheme is compared with that of T2AV mode in Figure 6. The latent of the conditioning frame is concatenated with the video latents along the temporal axis and receives its own temporal RoPE position. binary channel mask distinguishes the conditioning frame (value 1) from the frames to be denoised (value 0). In addition, we introduce two learnable embeddings in the token space, the Token Role Embeddings (TRE): one for the noisy video tokens and one for the reference frame. They are added to the input tokens and provide an additional learnable signal indicating whether token is noise or conditioning. Inference-time ablations showed that TRE has relatively weak effect on the result. Disabling the embeddings, or decomposing them into shared and role-specific components, changed the generations only slightly; noticeable effect appeared only when the rolespecific component was artificially amplified many times. This indicates that TRE carries discriminative information about token roles but is not the primary mechanism for recognizing the reference frame, since other cues largely duplicate its function. Setting the mask to one for all tokens almost completely blocked denoising, whereas an all-zero mask still allowed the video to be denoised but produced artifacts, mainly in the first latent frame. Changing the temporal RoPE position of the reference frame made the model use it at the specified position: reference with RoPE position t4, t8, and so on acted as condition for the corresponding part of the video. Thus, RoPE is the primary mechanism that binds the reference frame to position in the generated sequence, the mask explicitly separates conditioning tokens from tokens to be denoised, and TRE serves as an additional, partially redundant signal.

sections.title: 4.3 Supervised Fine-Tuning
sections.content: Supervised fine-tuning is performed in two stages on the SFT datasets described in Section 2 (see Table 1). In both stages, separate model is fine-tuned on each of the 11 domains. The domain-specific models are trained independently through both stages and are merged into model soup by uniform weight averaging only at the end of Stage 2. The same procedure is applied to both Kandinsky 6.0 Video Lite and Kandinsky 6.0 Video Pro. Stage 1 (visual quality). The goal of this stage is to improve visual quality. Training starts from the pre-trained checkpoint. The audio stream, the fusion modules, and the audio-text modules are frozen, and only the video loss is optimized: audio inputs still pass through the frozen audio stream but do not contribute to the loss. We use learning rate of 1 105 and the same mixture of prompt detail levels as in pre-training (long: 0.7, medium: 0.15, short: 0.1, shortest: 0.05). The model is trained in T2AV and I2AV modes (75% and 25% of steps, respectively). Training is stopped after 7,000 steps, the visually best iteration before overfitting begins. To evaluate the result of this stage, the 11 domain-specific checkpoints are uniformly averaged into an intermediate Stage 1 soup. This soup is used only for quality measurement and is not used in further training. Stage 2 (synchronization and lip-sync). This stage improves audio-video synchronization, with particular emphasis on lip-sync. Training continues separately from each domain-specific Stage 1 checkpoint rather than from the Stage 1 soup. All modules are unfrozen and trained with different learning rates: 1105 for the video stream and the shared modules and 1106 for the audio components. The loss is weighted sum of the video loss (weight 0.85), the audio loss (0.15), and new face loss (1.0). The face loss is the video loss restricted to the facial region in the latent space; it encourages more accurate lip-sync. As in Stage 1, 75% of steps are in T2AV mode and 25% in I2AV mode. After 5,000 steps, the 11 domain-specific checkpoints are uniformly averaged to obtain the final SFT model.

sections.title: 4.5 Distillation
sections.content: Following Kandinsky 5.0 [11], we split distillation into two complementary stages: 1. Trajectory distillation: the teachers sampling trajectory is compressed into few-step student. 2. Quality improvement: the perceptual fidelity lost during aggressive trajectory compression is recovered using real data and adversarial training.

sections.title: 4.5.1 Motivation and Method Selection
sections.content: For trajectory distillation, we evaluated several families of methods: DMD [52], DMD2 [53], SID [54], Phased Consistency [55], CFG distillation [56], π-Flow [57], and Parallel Decoding Distillation (PDD) [58]. Distribution-matching methods (DMD, DMD2, SID) provide direct objective for aligning the student and teacher distributions, but in our experiments they were prone to mode collapse and mode dropping. They also required substantially more GPUs because of expensive teacher evaluations, auxiliary score estimation, and optimization overhead. This cost is especially high for video, whose spatio-temporal latents are far more expensive to process than those of images. CFG distillation and consistency-based methods are simple and effective baselines, but we observed that they can alter the teachers generation behavior, including motion dynamics and the distribution of generated samples. They remained useful but were not flexible or performant enough for our few-step video generation setting. 25 We then evaluated two more recent trajectory-based methods, π-Flow and PDD. Of these, π-Flow showed the most reliable convergence and the best preservation of the teacher trajectory. Its imitation-learning formulation trains the student on-policy, i.e., on the states encountered during the students own rollout, which is the same distribution the student faces at inference. As with DMD, the quality of π-Flow is ultimately bounded by the teacher. Unlike distributionmatching methods, however, it avoids an aggressively mode-seeking objective: it encourages the student to reproduce the teachers local decisions along the trajectory, which substantially reduces mode collapse and mode dropping. The guided teacher trajectory can also be distilled directly, which removes the need for separate CFG distillation stage. For these reasons, we chose π-Flow for trajectory distillation. Trajectory compression alone does not fully preserve model quality: as the number of sampling steps decreases, generated videos become smoother and less detailed. This effect grows with more aggressive compression even when the semantic composition and global motion remain correct: the student loses high-frequency texture, local contrast, and fine spatial detail. Additional trajectory matching does not reliably fix this degradation. Therefore, the second stage uses real data and an adversarial objective to restore perceptual fidelity. We build on LADD [59] and introduce Simulated LADD (Sim-LADD), which aims to improve the realism of samples from the trajectory-compressed student. In standard LADD, the intermediate state xt used for adversarial training is obtained via the forward noising process. Following the on-policy formulation of DMD2, Sim-LADD instead obtains xt from the students own backward denoising rollout, so the discriminator sees the states actually encountered at inference, which reduces the traininference gap. Following DRaFT [60], the adversarial gradient can be propagated through the complete differentiable denoising chain rather than only through the final sample or single transition. In practice, truncated backpropagation through the final solver steps (DRaFT-k) provided comparable quality at substantially lower memory cost. We therefore use = 5, i.e., half of the students 10 NFE. 4.5.2 Distillation Pipeline 1. Trajectory compression via π-Flow. We distill the teacher into few-step student that requires only 10 function evaluations (NFEs). Among the methods we tried, π-Flow gave the best convergence, motion and audio fidelity, and trajectory alignment, without mode collapse. Because it formulates trajectory distillation as on-policy imitation learning, it directly absorbs the teachers CFGguided trajectory, which removes the need for separate CFG distillation stage. 2. Adversarial refinement via Sim-LADD. The trajectory-compressed student shows textural and perceptual degradation caused by the coarse discretization of the sampling trajectory. We refine this checkpoint with Sim-LADD: unlike standard LADD, which builds training states via forward diffusion, SimLADD uses actual backward rollouts of the student, which reduces the traininference mismatch (Figure 9). We backpropagate the adversarial gradient through the final sampling steps, following DRaFT-k. As in the original LADD, we apply stochastic re-noising to both real and generated latents before discriminator feature extraction. This stabilizes adversarial training, reduces discriminator overfitting, and removes the need for an explicit R1 gradient penalty such as the one used in APT [61]. 26 Figure 9: Rollout strategies for adversarial training. Top: standard LADD, where the intermediate state xt is obtained by forward noising of the clean sample x0 and denoised in single step with gradients. Middle: backward student rollout with gradients propagated through all denoising steps. Bottom: backward student rollout with gradients propagated only through the final steps. The two stages play complementary roles: π-Flow performs stable trajectory compression while preserving the teachers semantics, motion, and diversity, and Sim-LADD then uses real data and adversarial learning to recover the high-frequency detail and perceptual sharpness lost during compression. 4.5.3 Training Details The student policy network is initialized directly from the preStage 1: π-Flow distillation. trained teacher backbone and optimized with an on-policy imitation ℓ2 regression objective against the guided teacher velocity field. sections.title: 4.6 Super-Resolution
sections.content: A single SR-DiT model is trained jointly for 2 and 4 video super-resolution, using training pairs from both scales with equal sampling probability. The SR-DiT and the Latent Upscalers (LU), trained separately for each scale, are optimized independently. During SR-DiT training, the degraded LQ and HQ latents have matching spatial dimensions. For Real-ESRGAN-style degradations, this is achieved by bilinearly upsampling the lowresolution clip in pixel space before K-VAE encoding. The temporal degradation pipeline directly produces degraded clip at the HQ resolution. Each LU is trained to map low-resolution degraded latents to their high-resolution degraded counterparts and is used to prepare the input to SR-DiT at inference. 4.6.1 Training Data and Degradations The source videos come from the SR dataset described in Section 2.9. During dataset preparation, we extract video crops of the required spatial size, filter them, and construct degraded copies. An accepted crop serves as the HQ target, and its degraded counterpart provides the LQ input. Both versions are encoded with K-VAE and stored as paired video latents. For the 4K video collection and the Kandinsky 5.0 T2V Crop selection and online filtering. collection, we extract spatial crops of size 512 768, 512 512, or 768 512 pixels (height 28 width), retaining sequence of frames in each crop. Crop locations are selected using center cropping, random cropping, optical-flow-based selection, or selection of regions with high spatial detail. During data preparation, dark borders are excluded from the region available for cropping. Candidate video crops are checked for excessive dark content, visible banding, and compression artifacts using spatial and temporal quality measures. The crop-selection methods are tried in randomly sampled order, weighted by their configured probabilities. The first candidate that passes all checks is retained; videos for which no candidate passes are skipped. These crop-level checks complement the dataset-level quality filtering described in Section 2.9. We use two degradation pipelines to construct LQ counterparts from the accepted HQ crops. Real-ESRGAN-style degradation. We use video adaptation of the two-stage high-order degradation scheme of Real-ESRGAN [62]. The first stage applies blur, resizing, Gaussian or Poisson noise, JPEG compression, and video compression. The second stage repeats blur, resizing, noise, and JPEG compression, with weaker blur and noise settings. final block applies video compression and resizing to the target low-resolution size followed by optional sinc filtering; the order of these two components is randomized. Blur and resize parameters and noise strength are shared across frames, while noise is sampled independently per frame and JPEG quality varies gradually along the video. This pipeline degrades image quality without explicitly warping geometry or changing the frame sequence. The target low-resolution dimensions correspond to downscaling factor of 2 or 4 along each spatial axis, depending on the encoding configuration. For SR-DiT training, it is bilinearly upsampled back to the HQ dimensions before K-VAE encoding. The low-resolution version is also encoded and stored for LU training. Inspired by CreativeVR [63], this pipeline simulates CreativeVR-style temporal degradation. structural and temporal artifacts in generated video. We use the strong preset of our implementation. spatial grid warp is applied first, with displacement field interpolated between two randomly sampled grids over time. Next, three or four operators are selected and applied in random order: directional motion blur, adjacent-frame blending, stochastic frame dropping with interpolation, and spatio-temporal downsampling followed by reconstruction to the original frame count and spatial size. Motion-blur parameters and blending coefficients follow smooth temporal trajectories. The degraded video retains the HQ dimensions but contains distortions of geometry, motion, and fine detail. This full-resolution degraded version is encoded directly for SR-DiT training. separate low-resolution version is obtained by bilinear downsampling by factor of 2 or 4 and encoded for LU training. 4.6.2 SR-DiT Training Objective The SR-DiT is trained with flow matching to restore HQ latents from degraded LQ latents (Figure 11). In the first two training stages, pixel-space losses are applied only for 0.7. We use: Pixel L1 loss, with weight 0.6. 30 LPIPS perceptual loss with VGG backbone [64], with weight 0.35. High-Frequency Perception (HFP) loss adapted from [65]: L1 between the highfrequency Haar subbands (LH, HL, HH) of the reconstruction and target, with shared random spatial shift of 0 or 1 pixel along each axis. Its weight is 1.0. masked Fourier space (MFS) loss adapted from [66]: L1 between FFT amplitudes at the harmonic bins of 16-pixel grid, matching the spatial compression factor of K-VAE. Its weight is 1.0. HFP supervises high-frequency detail, while MFS specifically targets periodic grid artifacts. Together, they help suppress grid and checkerboard patterns. The total objective is = Lflow + (cid:88) λiLi. The settings above apply to the first two training stages; the distillation objective and its loss weights are described below. The anchor contains the first temporal slice of the ground-truth HQ latent, with HQ anchor. zeros at the remaining temporal positions. binary mask identifies the position containing the anchor. The anchor and mask are concatenated with xt along the channel dimension (Section 3.3.1). In the first two training stages, the anchor and its mask are jointly zeroed with probability 0.15, allowing the model to learn restoration without anchor conditioning. The current inference pipeline uses zero anchor and mask inputs. The conditioning interface also allows future inference variant to supply an HQ first-frame reference, for example using an image super-resolution model. 4.6.3 SR-DiT Training Stages The SR-DiT is trained in three stages on 8 NVIDIA H100 GPUs. All stages use AdamW with β = (0.9, 0.95), weight decay 103, gradient clipping at 1.0, and an LQ noise fraction of = 0.7. The 4 and 2 pair sets are sampled with equal probability, with source sequences of 2031 latent frames. Each GPU processes packed batch of 124 latent frames, equivalent to four 31-frame clips. Stage 3 additionally accumulates gradients over two microbatches. The SR-DiT is initialized from the text-free Kandinsky 5.0 Stage 1: training with dense attention. Video Lite (SFT) checkpoint and trained with dense attention. We use learning rate of 105 with 500 warmup steps, EMA decay 0.999, and timestep scheduler scale 5.0. The checkpoint at step 7,250 is used to initialize Stage 2. This stage takes approximately 4.5 days. To reduce attention cost, dense attention is replaced with Stage 2: NABLA fine-tuning. sparse NABLA attention [12]. We use top-CDF block selection with = 0.8, linearly annealed from 0.95 over the first 200 steps. This is combined with local neighborhood following sliding-tile attention (STA) [67], with window of 11 7 7 attention blocks along time, height, and width. Each spatial block contains 8 8 latent tokens. Training starts from the Stage 1 checkpoint at step 7,250 and runs for 6,000 steps with learning rate of 105, 200 warmup steps, and the same loss settings as Stage 1. This stage takes approximately 3 days. The model is distilled for inference with two SR-DiT calls using the Stage 3: π-Flow distillation. DX policy of π-Flow [57]. The frozen teacher and the student backbone are initialized from the Stage 2 checkpoint at step 6,000. The students output head is expanded to predict 10 velocity outputs and initialized by replicating the teachers output head. The denoising trajectory is divided into two segments. For each training sample, segment is selected, and its starting state is constructed using the HQ and noised LQ latents, with HQ anchor conditioning as in the preceding stages. The student makes one network call at the segment start. Its 10 velocity outputs are converted into grid of clean-latent predictions, which the DX policy interpolates to evaluate velocities within the segment without additional network calls. The teacher is evaluated at eight states along teacher-driven rollout within the selected segment. The DX loss is the MSE between the teacher velocity and the student policys velocity averaged over local integration window. The policy integration uses resolution of 128 substeps over the full trajectory, with minimum averaging window of three substeps. Pixel-space losses are computed from the policys clean-latent estimate at the segment start, ˆz0 = xt σtu, where σt is the shifted flow-matching timestep at the segment start and is the policy velocity. These losses directly supervise the clean-latent node at the segment start; the remaining nodes are supervised through the DX loss. They are applied at all noise levels with reduced weights: L1 0.05, LPIPS 0.026, HFP 0.16, and MFS 0.033. Decoding is limited to spatial crop corresponding to 256 256 pixels and at most four consecutive latent frames from one sample per GPU. Anchor dropout is set to 0.15 in Stages 1-2 and disabled in Stage 3. We use time shift of 3.5, final segment size scale of 0.5, learning rate of 106 with 100 warmup steps, gradient accumulation over two microbatches, and EMA decay 0.9999. The checkpoint used for inference is obtained after 750 distillation updates, corresponding to approximately 1.5 days. At inference, the distilled model operates with two network function evaluations (NFE = 2). Within each segment, the DX policy is integrated without additional network evaluations. 4.6.4 Latent Upscaler Training The LU is trained in degraded-to-degraded setting: the input is the K-VAE encoding of low-resolution degraded video, and the target is the encoding of its full-resolution degraded counterpart. The spatial grids differ by factor of 4 or 2 along each axis. The LU is thus trained to upsample the latent representation, while restoration of clean HQ content is handled by SR-DiT. The weak/synthetic training mixtures contain four groups: the Kandinsky 5.0 T2V collection with weak degradation, the 4K collection with weak Real-ESRGAN-style degradation, synthetic camera-motion clips constructed from images, and the 4K collection with synthetic temporal degradation. These mixtures contain approximately 218k pairs for 4 and 194k pairs for 2. Both models are trained on 4 GPUs using packed batches with budget of 124 latent frames per GPU, equivalent to four 31-frame clips. We use AdamW with β = (0.9, 0.95), weight decay 104, gradient clipping at 1.0, and EMA decay 0.99. The reconstruction objective combines latent-space Charbonnier loss (ϵ = 103, Losses. weight 1.0) with pixel-space L1 loss (weight 1.0). Pixel losses are computed by decoding matching crops of the predicted and target latents with the frozen K-VAE decoder; gradients propagate through the decoder to the LU. Pixel-space losses are evaluated every second training step for one sample per GPU, using spatial latent crop of 1624 cells and the first nine latent frames. LPIPS is disabled as training loss. 32 Temporal supervision matches frame-to-frame differences between the prediction and target. In the initial 4 run, the latent temporal L1 loss has weight 0.1. After 50k steps, its weight is increased to 0.5, and decoded pixel temporal L1 loss with weight 1.0 is added. The 2 model uses these latter temporal loss settings from the start. 4 model. All parameters except the output heads are initialized from the corresponding KVAE decoder modules, including the input projection. Only the output heads are optimized for the first 100 steps; the transferred layers are then included in training. Training consists of three consecutive runs: 50k steps with base learning rate of 2.2 104, 40k steps with 1.1 104, and final 10k-step polishing run with 1.1 105. The temporal-loss changes described above are introduced in the second run. We use µP-inspired learning-rate scaling: hidden and output convolution weights receive the base learning rate multiplied by 512/Cin, where Cin is the number of input channels. Input projections, normalization and modulation parameters, and biases retain the base rate. Training takes approximately 60 hours on 4 GPUs. The 2 branch is initialized by copying modules from the trained 4 model (Sec2 model. tion 3.3.2). The 4 path is frozen, and all parameters of the 2 branch are optimized from the first step. The model is trained for 40k steps with base learning rate of 2.2 104, followed by 10k-step polishing run with 2.2 105. The first 20k steps use the stronger-degradation pair set; the subsequent runs use the weak/synthetic mixture described above. Training takes approximately two days on 4 GPUs. 4.6.5 Validation SR-DiT metrics. Generated videos have no paired HQ ground truth. We therefore monitor restoration quality using no-reference quality metrics and additional spatial and temporal diagnostics: MUSIQ [68] is an image quality metric. We use the KonIQ-10k checkpoint, score decoded frames independently, and average the scores over frames and clips; higher is better. As frame-level metric, it does not directly assess temporal consistency. DOVER [33] is video quality metric combining technical and aesthetic branches. The technical branch processes sampled fragments, while the aesthetic branch processes spatially downscaled video. We report the fused, normalized score in [0, 1]; higher is better. Warp error measures motion-compensated differences between adjacent frames. We estimate forward and backward optical flow with RAFT [69], warp one frame onto the other, and compute the mean absolute residual over valid, non-occluded pixels; lower is better. The metric is sensitive to temporal inconsistencies, but also to image detail and optical-flow accuracy. Smooth outputs can receive low errors, so the score must be interpreted together with spatial quality. Laplacian artifact score measures excess high-frequency response in the SR output relative to the upsampled LQ input. Sobel edges in the LQ frame are used to exclude natural edges, restricting scoring to smooth regions; lower is better. The score helps identify grid and checkerboard artifacts, but can also respond to newly reconstructed detail. We additionally report CLIP-IQA [70], with higher scores indicating better predicted image quality. MUSIQ and DOVER were developed for natural-image and user-generated-video quality assessment, respectively, and their scores may not fully reflect SR-specific artifacts. 33 We therefore use these metrics as complementary indicators, rather than treating any single score as complete quality measure. Final SR quality assessment and checkpoint selection are based on side-by-side human evaluation at both the tile and full-frame levels. The source videos are generated by Kandinsky 5.0 Video Lite (T2V, SFT, SR-DiT validation sets. 5 s). We use two separate sets of 912 video crops each. sections.title: 5 Inference
sections.content: Figure 12 summarizes the output resolutions supported at inference (given as width height). In SD mode, the output of the base model (864480, 480864, or 512512) is returned as is. In Full HD mode, the base-model output is upscaled by factor of 2.25 with the super-resolution model (Section 3.3) and then downscaled to 19201080, 10801920, or 10801080. An HD mode (1280720) is obtained in the same way by downsampling the super-resolution output  (Table 6)  . Figure 12: Output resolutions of Kandinsky 6.0 Video at inference. In SD mode, the basemodel output is returned without changes; in Full HD mode, it is upscaled 2.25 by the superresolution model and then downscaled to the target Full HD resolution. The SR inference pipeline is shown in Figure 13. The figure illustrates the common encoding, tiling, upscaling, and decoding stages, with the Euler denoising loop used by the predistillation model. The final distilled model replaces this loop with π-Flow DX policy sampling. The pipeline consists of the following steps: 1. Pre-upscaling (only for 2.25). The generated video is bilinearly upscaled by 1.125 in pixel space, with the dimensions aligned to the spatial compression factor of K-VAE (16 px). For example, an 864480 video becomes 976544. The 2 route is then applied. 2. Encoding. The whole clip is encoded with K-VAE once. 121-frame video is mapped to 31 latent frames. 3. Latent tiling. The latent representation is split into overlapping spatial tiles, using minimum overlap of 25%. Each tile covers the full temporal extent of the clip. For 512 768 working resolution, input tiles contain 16 24 latent cells for the 2 route and 8 12 cells for the 4 route, corresponding to source regions of 256384 and 128192 pixels, respectively. For square content, the corresponding input tiles contain 16 16 or 8 8 latent cells. 4. Latent upscaling. The scale-specific Latent Upscaler brings each tile to the SR-DiT working resolution: 32 48 latent cells for landscape content or 32 32 cells for square content. Portrait content uses the transposed spatial dimensions. 36 Figure 13: Tiled SR inference with the Latent Upscaler. The LQ video is encoded once with K-VAE and split into overlapping latent tiles. Each tile is upscaled by the 2 or 4 LU, refined by SR-DiT, decoded, and merged using Hann-window blending. The denoising loop shown corresponds to the pre-distillation model; the final distilled model replaces this loop with πFlow DX policy sampling using two network evaluations (NFE = 2). 5. Denoising. The upscaled LQ latent is partially noised using the same noise fraction as in training (s = 0.7), giving the starting state at = 1: z1 = (cid:112) 1 s2 LQ + ε, ε (0, I). The Stage 2 model uses an Euler sampler, typically with 48 network evaluations (NFE), predicting the velocity at each step and updating the latent until = 0. The final Stage 3 model instead uses π-Flow DX policy sampling [57] with two network evaluations (NFE = 2). At the start of each of two trajectory segments, SR-DiT predicts 10 velocity outputs, which are converted into clean-latent nodes defining DX policy. The policy is integrated within the segment using network-free Euler substeps: velocities are computed from the interpolated nodes without additional SR-DiT evaluations. Thus, NFE = 2 denotes two network evaluations per tile, rather than two Euler integration steps. Both models are text-free, with classifier-free guidance disabled. The HQ anchor and its mask are set to zero at inference. 6. Decoding and blending. Each restored latent tile is decoded with K-VAE. The overlapping decoded tiles are combined using normalized Hann-window weights to reduce boundary seams. 7. Final resizing. The assembled SR output is resized without cropping to the target resolution 37 (Figure 12). Depending on the route, the downscaling factor ranges from approximately 1.01 (1952 1088 1920 1080) to 1.42 (1024 1024 720 720). Kandinsky 6.0 Video uses the 2.25 routes to produce Full HD output (Figure 12). The SR pipeline also supports HD and 2K output via the 2 and 4 routes. sections.title: 6 Optimizations and Consumer GPU Deployment
sections.content: Throughout this section, Lite and Pro denote Kandinsky 6.0 Video Lite and Kandinsky 6.0 Video Pro, and SD, HD, and Full HD denote the three operating modes defined in Section 5; configuration such as Pro SD refers to the Kandinsky 6.0 Video Pro model in SD mode. All base-model measurements in this section are obtained with the full, non-distilled model. Peak allocated memory during Pro SD run reaches 72.8 GiB, which does not fit on any consumer GPU. Both Lite and Pro run on 32, 24, and 16 GB cards through weight offloading: only two transformer blocks reside on the GPU at time, the rest are streamed from CPU memory during the forward pass. The offloading mechanism itself is identical for both model sizes; only the number of blocks and the resulting resident footprint differ. The mathematical model is unchanged. Peak memory drops by about 3.4 for Pro at SD and about 1.8 for Pro at HD and Full HD; for Lite the reduction is approximately 2 at SD and 1.1 at HD and Full HD. Total generation time on the reference H100 changes by few percent.

sections.title: 6.1 Block Offloading
sections.content: The transfer of the next block is overlapped with the computation of the current one on separate CUDA stream. Embeddings, RoPE, and output projections remain resident on the GPU for the duration of the DiT stage. When MagCache skips step, the weights of the skipped blocks are not transferred at all. Peak PyTorch allocated memory is summarized in Table 7. These values are measured with the default SR decoding configuration; the presets described below report lower peaks because they use shorter SR decode segment and, at 16 GB, additional spatial splitting of the SR decoder. The two values in the HD/Full HD row correspond to the two base geometries (768432 and 864480), not to range across repeats. Resident Block offload Pro, SD Pro, HD / Full HD Lite, SD Lite, HD / Full HD 44.544. 72.8 72.8 43.5 21.7 39.639.8 21.7 39.539.8 The mode is inference-only. It is not compatible with CUDA graphs, whole-model compilation, or externally exported weights, including the Magi SR backend [71]. PyTorch 2.13 is required: with PyTorch 2.10, offloading breaks the compiled forward pass. Base-model outputs match the resident variant to within the numerical epsilon of the data type: video at SD, and both frames and audio at HD and Full HD.

sections.title: 6.3 Inference Acceleration
sections.content: Four mechanisms are in use. Regional compilation. Base DiT blocks are compiled individually through torch.compile. The model is not compiled as whole. Compilation is enabled in the Pro configuration. MagCache. MagCache [72] skips subset of sampling steps based on the magnitude of the update. On Pro SD it evaluates 49 of 100 forwards and roughly halves the base stage. Attention backends. On the H100 visual attention is computed with FlashAttention 3 [73]. On all other tested GPUs the consumer cards (RTX 4090, 5060 Ti, 5080, 5090), the RTX PRO 6000 workstation card, and the A100 80 GB datacenter card visual self-attention is computed with SageAttention2++ [74]; FlashAttention 3 does not support these architectures. Text blocks and cross-attention use FlashAttention 2 [75]. SR uses its own attention mechanism from the checkpoint, including NABLA [12], and does not switch together with the base. SR VAE compilation. The SR VAE decoder is compiled regionally and by default roughly halves the SR stage. Disabling it saves small amount of memory, from 22.9 to 20.3 GiB.

sections.content: SR memory settings segment length, spatial strips, offloading change the output at the level of rounding noise. Approximately 12% of pixels differ by one brightness level, PSNR is around 57 dB, and no visible structure or seams appear at segment boundaries. Bitwise equality of SR frames between offloading modes to the epsilon of the data type has not been established. Disabling decoder compilation does not remove the difference. NF4 quantization of the text encoder is the only preset setting that changes the clip itself: different textual representation produces different video. It is enabled only at 16 GB. sections.title: 7.1 Benchmarking
sections.content: We evaluate the final Kandinsky 6.0 Video checkpoints on VABench [21], benchmark for text-to-audio-video generation that covers audio quality, cross-modal alignment, synchronization, realism, and expressiveness. Results are reported for Kandinsky 6.0 Video Pro and Kandinsky 6.0 Video Lite after RL post-training, both at 512 768 resolution, alongside LTX 2.5 in its two-stage Full HD configuration. Scores are listed in Table 11 and visualized as radar chart in Figure 14. Kandinsky 6.0 Video Pro leads on speech quality, audio aesthetics, text-video and audiovideo alignment, lip-sync accuracy, desynchronization, and visual realism. Kandinsky 6.0 Video Lite shows the strongest results on text-audio alignment, audio realism, and the audio and visual quality scores. LTX 2.5 retains an advantage on the VLM-judged alignment and expressiveness scores, and on word error rate. The word error rate is not part of VABench. We compute it separately on the speech subset: audio is transcribed with Qwen3-ASR-1.7B, punctuation is removed from both the ASR output and the reference prompt, and WER is computed with the jiwer library. Note that this differs from the WER reported in Section 4.4, which uses Whisper-large-v3, one of the RL reward models; the two numbers are not directly comparable and should not be read as conflicting.

sections.title: 7.2 Human Evaluation
sections.content: 7.2.1 Methodology The human evaluation is performed as side-by-side (SBS) comparison of pairs of videos generated from the same prompt by two different models. Visual questions (audio disabled): 1. Overall Visual Quality. Which video is preferred visually, without taking the prompt into account? The annotator considers composition, lighting, colour and contrast, and overall visual appeal. 2. Artifacts and Semantic Breaks. Which video contains fewer artifacts and fewer unintended semantic breaks? Artifacts include extra limbs, fingers, unrelated objects, watermarks, unrelated text, grain, flicker, texture changes without reason, and loss of face identity. Semantic breaks include unintended object transformations and sudden appearances or disappearances of objects. The prompt is available for reference to distinguish artifacts from requested content. 3. Motion Realism and Physics. Which video has more realistic object motion and better adheres to the rules of the physical world? The annotator evaluates trajectories of limbs, head, and facial expression, body coherence, and physical plausibility of object interactions. The prompt is available for reference. 4. Visual Prompt Following. Which video better follows the prompt, ignoring the audiorelated part of the description? The evaluation considers, in priority order, the number of objects, their quantities, properties, spatial arrangement, actions, and on-screen text. 5. Camera Motion. Which video correctly reproduces the camera motion requested in the prompt? If several camera motions are requested, their count is compared. If the prompt does not specify any camera motion, the question is marked as not applicable. Audio and audio-visual questions (audio enabled): 6. Speech Quality. Which video has better speech quality? The annotator evaluates intelligibility, naturalness of voice and articulation, and, if singing is requested, whether the content is actually sung. Lip-sync and facial expression are evaluated only when the speaker is on screen. 7. Audio-Video Synchronization. Which video has less desynchronization between audio and visuals? Temporal alignment is evaluated between sound events and their visual counterparts (e.g., speech and lip movement, impact and contact, door opening and sound). Desynchronization explicitly requested in the prompt is not penalized. 43 8. Overall Audio Quality. Which video has better overall audio quality? The annotator evaluates audio defects such as muffled sound, extreme quietness, harsh clipping, unexpected interruptions, noise, and artifacts. The correspondence between audio and prompt is not evaluated here. 9. Sound Prompt Following. Which videos audio better corresponds to the prompt? The annotator evaluates how accurately the requested sounds (speech, sound effects, background music, ambience) are reproduced. Missing requested sounds, wrong sounds, or wrong spoken text are counted as errors. 10. User Task Solving. Which video better solves the users task as whole? The annotator evaluates visual and audio logic, coherence, and whether the generation can be used as finished result. For contradictory prompts, the video offering the better creative synthesis is preferred. Image-to-Video additional question: 11. Reference Image Correspondence. sections.title: 8 Examples
sections.content: This section presents qualitative results that are difficult to convey through quantitative benchmarks alone. Video and synchronized audio generation cannot be fully represented on the printed page: the reader cannot play back the generated audio track or observe the temporal alignment between sound and motion. We therefore rely on two complementary forms of illustration. For audio-visual examples (Section 8.1), each figure shows sequence of frames sampled from single 5-second generation at 24 fps, together with the waveform of the corresponding audio track. The waveform makes two properties visible at glance. First, the audio is synchronized with the video: impact sounds produce spikes at the exact frames where the impact occurs, and speech amplitude follows the movements of the lips. Second, the generated audio is semantically consistent with the visual scene: the model produces the sound 54 of the objects and actions it has generated, not generic ambient noise. These properties are further confirmed by the side-by-side human evaluation and by the VABench results reported in Section 7, where Kandinsky 6.0 Video is competitive with leading audio-video generation models on both synchronization and speech quality. Super-resolution examples are provided in Section 8.2. All examples in this section are generated by Kandinsky 6.0 Video Pro unless stated otherwise. Examples of generated videos with their audio tracks are available in the public release materials at https://github.com/kandinskylab/kandinsky-6.

sections.title: 9.1 Image and Video Generation
sections.content: Diffusion models [1, 2] and flow matching [3, 76] have become the dominant paradigm for visual generation. Latent diffusion [4] made high-resolution synthesis computationally tractable, and transformer backbones [6, 77] have largely replaced convolutional U-Nets in recent systems. The Kandinsky family of text-to-image models followed this trajectory over several generations [78, 79, 80]. Early video diffusion models extended image generators with temporal layers [81, 82, 83], while more recent systems train spatio-temporal diffusion transformers at scale [84, 85, 86, 9, 10, 87, 88]. Within the Kandinsky line, architectural design choices for text-to-video pipelines were studied in [89, 90], followed by the CrossDiT-based Kandinsky 5.0 family [11], on which Kandinsky 6.0 Video directly builds. Other works address individual components of video generation pipelines, including efficient attention for long spatio-temporal sequences [12, 67, 91], autoencoder training without characteristic artifacts [92], explicit temporal control in video diffusion transformers [93], and temporally correlated generative priors for video-to-video tasks [94]. Culture-specific generation and its evaluation are supported by dedicated datasets and benchmarks [46, 47], which underlie the Russian Cultural Code data used in this work (Section 2).

sections.title: 9.2 Joint Audio-Video Generation
sections.content: Audio and video have long been generated separately or sequentially, for example by synthesizing soundtrack for given video [48]. Closed commercial systems such as Veo 3.1 [8] and Sora 2 [13] demonstrated that both modalities can be generated jointly with natural lip synchronization and sound effects. Open research models pursue the same goal with range of designs: temporally aligned flow-based generation [15], hierarchical spatio-temporal synchronization priors [16], unified tri-modal transformers [17], and dual-stream transformers with cross-modal fusion [49, 18]. Large-scale systems such as ALIVE [14], MiniMax-H3 [19], and Cosmos 3 [20] further extend joint audio-video generation. Kandinsky 6.0 Video follows the dualstream design but initializes the video stream from pretrained video model and trains the audio stream from scratch (Section 3). Joint audio-video models can also be extended with additional conditioning, such as reference-based voice cloning [95]. Progress in this area is measured by dedicated benchmarks for audio-video quality and synchronization [21, 22, 23].

sections.title: 9.3 Post-Training and Few-Step Sampling
sections.content: Supervised fine-tuning on curated data and averaging of fine-tuned weights (model soups) [96, 97] are common ways to improve the quality of pretrained generators. Reinforcement learning further aligns diffusion and flow models with human preferences and reward models [98, 99, 100, 101]; OmniNFT [24] adapts this approach to joint audio-video generation. To reduce the number of sampling steps, prior work has explored progressive distillation [102], consistency models [103, 104, 55], distribution matching [52, 53, 54], adversarial distillation [105, 59, 61], and policy-based imitation distillation [57].

sections.title: 9.4 Video Super-Resolution
sections.content: Real-world super-resolution models are commonly trained on synthetic degradations that imitate blur, noise, resizing, and compression [62]. Diffusion-based approaches add strong generative priors and reduce the number of sampling steps [65, 66], and recent work addresses 61 structural and temporal artifacts specific to generated videos [63] as well as temporally consistent video-to-video restoration [94]. Our SR model operates in latent space and combines deterministic latent upscaler with text-free diffusion transformer distilled to two network evaluations (Section 3.3).

sections.title: 10 Conclusion
sections.content: We presented Kandinsky 6.0 Video, family of foundation models for synchronized text-toaudio-video and image-to-audio-video generation, comprising Kandinsky 6.0 Video Lite (3B parameters) and Kandinsky 6.0 Video Pro (29B parameters). Both models use dual-stream CrossDiT architecture in which video stream inherited from Kandinsky 5.0 and an audio stream trained from scratch are connected by blockwise bidirectional cross-attention. The models are trained with continuous pre-training, first separately for each modality and then jointly, followed by domain-specific supervised fine-tuning merged into model soup, reinforcement learning adapted from OmniNFT, and two-stage distillation (π-Flow followed by adversarial refinement) to 10 function evaluations. separate latent-space super-resolution model, consisting of Latent Upscaler and text-free SR-DiT distilled to two network evaluations, raises the output resolution to Full HD. Block offloading and memory presets make both models usable on consumer GPUs with 1632 GB of memory. In side-by-side human evaluation, Kandinsky 6.0 Video Pro clearly outperforms its predecessor, Kandinsky 5.0 Video Pro, and is preferred over LTX 2.5 in visual quality and speech quality. Compared with proprietary systems, the results are mixed: the model is competitive with Kling 2.6 and Veo 3.1 Fast, with strengths that differ by criterion, while MiniMax H3 and Seedance 2.0 remain stronger on visual criteria; Kandinsky 6.0 Video Pro stays competitive on speech quality and audio-video synchronization. On VABench, Kandinsky 6.0 Video Pro achieves the best scores among the evaluated models (Kandinsky 6.0 Video Lite and LTX 2.5) in speech quality, audio aesthetics, text-video and audio-video alignment, lip-sync, desynchronization, and visual realism. Reinforcement learning reduces the word error rate of generated speech by 47% for the Pro model. The models have several limitations. They generate clips of up to 5 seconds, the base generation runs at SD resolution with Full HD obtained through super-resolution, and gap remains to the strongest proprietary systems in visual quality and overall audio quality. Natural directions for future work include longer clips, higher native resolution, and additional reference-based conditioning. We release the model weights, source code, and diffusers integration under the MIT license to support further research on multimodal generation.

sections.title: Ethical Considerations
sections.content: Kandinsky 6.0 Video is intended to support research, education, and creative work, including content production, prototyping, and accessible tools for visual and audio storytelling. We believe that openly available generative models should be developed and used responsibly, with respect for human rights, personal dignity, and applicable law. Models that produce realistic video with synchronized speech and lip movements carry specific risks. They can be misused to create misleading or deceptive content, to impersonate real individuals, to spread disinformation, or to facilitate fraud and harassment. We do not support and explicitly discourage any such use. In particular, the models should not be used to depict real people without their consent, to imitate persons voice or appearance for deceptive purposes, to generate content that sexualizes minors or depicts non-consensual intimate imagery, to promote violence, hatred, or discrimination, or to infringe intellectual property rights. 62 We encourage users and downstream developers to clearly label generated content as synthetic, to comply with the laws and regulations of their jurisdictions, including those governing personal data, image and voice rights, and the disclosure of AI-generated media, and to implement appropriate safeguards, such as content moderation, when deploying the models in public-facing products. Like other models trained on large-scale data, Kandinsky 6.0 Video may reflect biases present in its training data, including uneven representation of demographic groups, cultures, and languages. Its outputs may also contain factual, physical, or cultural inaccuracies and should not be treated as depictions of real events. We encourage the research community to study these limitations and to report problematic behavior.
